column4: The section's و س م is a brand that makes a creature known; God promises to brand the hostile denier on the snout, making the identifying mark punitive rather than honorific.
The section explicitly reads this as the Qur'anic counterpart to وسم: the ruined town contains signs for the مُتَوَسِّمِين, people able to read traces and marks.
The needy are known by their سِيمَا although they do not beg insistently; this gives the section's readable mark a quiet social form rather than a literal burn.
The people on the heights recognize every group by their سِيمَا; the verse stages precisely the identification by an outward distinguishing mark developed in the section.
The people on the heights recognize particular men by their سِيمَا before addressing them, making the mark a basis for discernment and judgment.
Their سِيمَا is in their faces from the trace of prostration; a bodily trace visibly identifies worship, joining the section's mark to worship under God's name.
Criminals are recognized by their سِيمَا and seized; this is the adverse judicial counterpart to the section's claim that an imprint lets one be known.
The clay stones are مُسَوَّمَة, marked by their Lord for the transgressors; the same brand vocabulary becomes a precisely assigned punishment.
The angels' stones are مُسَوَّمَة for the excessive; this repeats the image of a mark that distinguishes and designates its object.
The promised angels are مُسَوِّمِينَ, marked or bearing distinguishing marks in battle; it realizes the section's dictionary image of a rider's battle badge.
God makes عَلَامَات, then stars by which people find their way. Raised landmarks and guiding signs give the section's flag-like علم a concrete Qur'anic scene.
Ships move on the sea like الْأَعْلَام, towering visible markers; the section's banner word becomes a large, recognizable form on the water.
The ships raised on the sea are like الْأَعْلَام. Repeating the marker image makes their height and visibility part of what identifies them.
God teaches Adam all the names, joining الاسم to عَلَّم: naming is knowledge, exactly as the section says a name is what makes a thing knowable.
Adam informs the angels of the names, completing 2:31: the taught names are publicly articulated so the things can be identified, and God contrasts this with the angels' limited knowledge.
Yahya is given a name for which God says He has made no prior سَمِيّ. The name distinguishes this promised child by denying an earlier namesake.
After commanding worship and patience, the verse asks whether one knows for God a سَمِيّ. It makes the source's namesake sense a test of whether any equal can bear the divine name.
God's most beautiful names are to be used in calling on Him. This directly extends the opening name from a label into an act of invocation.
Call on Allah or call on al-Rahman: the verse joins the two names in the opening and says the most beautiful names belong to Him, so the name directs a real call.
Allah has no god but Him and possesses the most beautiful names. The verse anchors the section's claim that the greatest name is a name of the uniquely worshipped referent.
Allah is Creator, Originator, and Fashioner, and His are the most beautiful names; the names identify through the acts and qualities that make their bearer known.
God has named the community Muslims before and in this revelation. A collective name here publicly identifies a people and their witness-bearing role.
Calling adopted children by their fathers' names is declared more just before God. The verse makes the name a safeguard of true relation and recognition.
Jesus announces a later messenger whose name is Ahmad. The stated name is an identifying sign within the announcement, rather than an empty title.
Solomon's letter begins with بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. At the head of writing, the name identifies both the letter's source and the authority in whose name it speaks.
Noah tells the passengers that the ark's course and mooring are بسم الله. The name is set over a concrete undertaking, as the section says an action is placed under the known sign.
Read in the name of the Lord who created: reading itself begins under the name, and creation supplies the identifying act behind the Lord's designation.
Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High. Name, Lord, and elevation are explicitly together, matching the section's derivation of ism from height.
Blessed is the name of the Lord of majesty and generosity. The verse makes the name itself exalted, directly echoing the section's raised sign.
In houses God has permitted to be raised, His name is remembered. Physical elevation and the utterance of the name are joined in one worship scene.
God says He raised Muhammad's mention. This is the section's good name spreading among people rendered as an explicitly elevated remembrance.
God grants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob a lofty truthful mention. A high reputation gives the source's raised-name image a concrete Qur'anic form.
Abraham asks for a truthful mention among later people. The request clarifies that a good name is a continuing recognizable trace after its bearer.
Glorifying the name of the Great Lord makes the name the object of exaltation, parallel to 87:1's Most High Lord.
The closing command to glorify the name of the Great Lord repeats the elevated-name action after the surah's scenes of creation and judgment.
The surah closes by commanding glorification of the Great Lord's name, preserving the connection between the spoken name and divine greatness.
Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself wholly to Him. The name leads into the patient worship that 19:65 also connects with knowing its unique bearer.
Remember the name of your Lord morning and evening. The recurrent spoken name makes invocation a continuing orientation, not a one-time label.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays; this pairs the name with the worship response developed beside 87:1 in the section.
The return of the Ark is specified as the sign of Saul's kingship. A concrete object functions as the public mark by which an otherwise disputed claim is recognized.
Outer garments are prescribed so women may be recognized and not harmed. Dress becomes an outward, protective sign of identity, like the section's mark made for knowing.
God will show His signs and people will recognize them. The verse directly links displayed signs with recognition, the function the section assigns to names and marks.
Many signs in the heavens and earth are passed by while people turn away. It gives the section's whole creation-as-sign claim its opposite human response: failing to read what is visible.
The diversity of languages and colors is among God's signs. Created differences themselves become distinguishing marks through which the plurality of the worlds is known.
Fruits, mountains, and paths appear in differing colors, including intensely black. The verse makes visible differentiation within creation into signs a reader can observe.
People, animals, and livestock likewise differ in colors, and those with knowledge fear God. Species and visible distinctions meet the section's claim that each kind of creation is a sign.
God promises to show signs on the horizons and in people themselves until truth becomes clear. It generalizes the section's readable mark from a brand to world and self.
The creation of the heavens, earth, and the creatures dispersed through them are signs. This most directly matches the section's reading of the worlds and every created kind as markers.
The heavens and earth contain signs for believers; creation is presented as something whose visible order points beyond itself.
In human creation and the creatures God spreads are signs for people of certainty. The verse makes living kinds, central to the section's عالمين image, readable evidence.
The alternation of night and day, rain, revived earth, and turning winds are signs for people who reason; changing natural patterns are ordered markers rather than mute events.
In the earth are signs for those certain in faith. The ground beneath the reader becomes part of the world the section calls a field of signs.
There are signs in yourselves as well; the verse turns the reader from external marks to the self as a recognizable sign.
Mary and her son are made a sign for the worlds. A living human relation becomes an ayah addressed to all the created kinds named by عالمين.
The son of Mary and his mother are made a sign and placed on an elevated, settled place with water. The verse joins a living sign to the section's imagery of height.
Noah and the people of the ark are made a sign for the worlds. The surviving vessel and its people become a public trace through which a later world recognizes the event.
Pharaoh's body is preserved so that it may be a sign for those after him. A body left visible becomes an enduring identifying trace and warning.
God makes stars for navigation in land and sea and details signs for people who know. Celestial markers perform the guiding function that 16:16 assigns to landmarks.
The creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding; the world is explicitly presented as discernible indication.
Salih calls the she-camel God's sign and commands his people to leave it to feed. A particular living creature is publicly set apart as a sign, not simply an animal.
The aftermath of the town's destruction is again called a sign for believers. It confirms that the readable traces in 15:75 are not merely private inference but a disclosed sign.
The speakers say they descend only by the Lord's command; this supplies the immediate voice and command-context for 19:65's worship of the one without a namesake.
The town is overturned and pelted with marked-like baked clay; this is the concrete ruined scene that 15:75 says the مُتَوَسِّمُون read, while 15:75 supplies the explicit reader.
The destroyed place remains on an established road. Its location makes the aftermath in 15:74–75 available as a trace to be encountered and read.
The queen first identifies the object cast to her as a noble letter; 27:30 then gives its named header, so this verse supplies the recognitional setting for the opening formula.
Those who remember God read heaven and earth's creation as not purposeless. It gives the responsive act of understanding that completes the signs named in 3:190.
Rain brings forth plants, fruit, and their ripening, and the verse asks observers to look because these are signs. Observable growth becomes a readable display within creation.
The sun's radiance and the moon's measured phases let people know the count of years, and are detailed as signs for people who know. Celestial order serves recognition and knowledge.
The succession of night and day and what God created in the heavens and earth are signs for the reverent. It extends the section's world-as-sign vision to recurring time.
Night and day are made two signs, with the day made seeing so people can seek bounty and know number and reckoning. Their contrast is designed to be read.
God creates the heavens and earth in truth, and this contains a sign for believers. The verse supplies the broad creation-to-sign relation underlying عالمين.
The immediately preceding referent is called a عِلْم for the Hour, a knowledge-marker in the text. This lets the section's علم move from knowing an object to an event that signals what is coming.
The angels announce a word from God whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary. The stated name and title distinguish the announced person before his appearance.
Peoples and tribes are made so that people may know one another. Human differentiation has a stated recognitional purpose, a social parallel to the section's distinguishing sign.
The Sacred House contains clear signs, including Abraham's standing place. A fixed place is named as a visible sign that identifies the sacred site and its history.
Safa and Marwah are among God's شعائر, public sacred symbols. Their named, visible locations show how a place can function as a sign within worship.
Honoring God's شعائر is linked to piety of hearts. The verse connects an outward sacred sign with the inward recognition to which it ought to lead.
The sacrificial camels are among God's شعائر, and His name is pronounced over them while standing. A visible ritual marker and the divine name converge in one act.
The hunter is told to mention God's name over what trained animals catch. An ordinary act is made answerable to the name, extending the beginning-under-the-name pattern.
Believers are told to eat what God's name has been mentioned over. The named act gives the source's opening formula a daily ritual form.
Pilgrims are to mention God's name on appointed days over the livestock He provided. The name is spoken over a concrete provision and communal act.
Every community receives rites so it may mention God's name over the livestock He has provided. Naming frames sacrifice across communities, not just Noah's particular journey.
Not eating what God's name was not mentioned over makes the boundary visible: an action without the name is described as defiance, reversing the marked act of 6:118.
When Allah alone is mentioned, some hearts recoil, while mention of others pleases them. The verse exposes competing names as signals of allegiance rather than neutral labels.
Hud calls the objects of worship mere names his people and their fathers named, with no authority from God. These are the section's raised signs without a real referent beneath them.
Joseph says the objects worshipped are only names named by people and their fathers. The verse directly supplies the section's image of an elevated label unsupported by what it claims to identify.
The alleged deities are only names named by people and their fathers, with no proof sent down. This repeats the boundary between a name that discloses and one that merely circulates.
When told to prostrate to al-Rahman, they ask what al-Rahman is. Rejection of the name blocks the worship and recognition that the opening name invites.
